transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

Whether it's worth fixing depends entirely on what's failed, and the good news is the two most common causes of this are cheap. Since it still fills and drains, the electronics and water side are clearly working. It's just the drive to the drum that's stopped. If it turns out to be the drive belt or the motor's carbon brushes, it's usually well worth doing even at 9 years old. Both are inexpensive parts, and a reasonably handy owner can often fit them. If it's the motor itself, the control board or worn drum bearings, the repair cost starts to approach the price of a new budget machine. At that age, replacing it is often the more sensible choice. - The drive belt has come off or snapped. This is very common, and the drum then sits still while the motor spins away.
• Worn carbon brushes. Many Indesits of this age typically use a brushed motor, and after 9 years the brushes wearing down to nothing is a classic way for the drum to just stop.
• Something jamming the drum, such as a bra wire or coin caught between the drum and tub, or seized bearings.
• Less likely: the motor itself, its cut-out, or the control board. 1. Switch off and unplug the machine, open the door and turn the drum by hand. If it turns freely and smoothly, the drum is fine and it's a drive problem (belt or brushes). If it's stiff, rough, grinding or jams part-way, it's mechanical, either a trapped object or the bearings.
2. Listen as you turn it for anything sliding or scraping.
3. Plug back in and start a wash, then listen once it's filled and should be tumbling. If you can hear the motor whirring but the drum doesn't move, that points strongly to the belt. If there's no motor sound at all, or just a click or hum, brushes or the motor become more likely. If the drum turns freely, the next step is usually a look at the belt behind the back panel, done with the machine unplugged. Let me know how the drum feels and what you hear, and I'll tell you which way it's pointing.

Thanks. I've unplugged it and turned the drum by hand: it turns freely and quietly, with no scraping or rumble. I also had a look for anything stuck between the drum and tub and found nothing. When I started a wash I could hear the relays clicking but no motor noise at all. Once I did smell something hot and electrical a few weeks ago, but not since.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. That's really useful, and it narrows things down a lot. The relays clicking shows the control board is trying to start the motor. No motor sound at all means the motor isn't running, so it isn't the belt: a slipped belt would still let you hear the motor whirring. Put together with the hot electrical smell, the most likely cause is worn carbon brushes. On a brushed motor, which Indesits of this age typically have, brushes that wear down start to spark and give off exactly that kind of smell. I'm fairly confident of that, though not certain. Close behind are a scorched wire or connector at the motor, or a failed motor winding. Least likely is the motor drive circuit on the control board. Because there's been that electrical burning smell, please don't run it again until a qualified engineer has checked it. Keep it unplugged. If it's the brushes, the problem is sparking at the motor, and a scorched connector could be involved too. An engineer needs to confirm what's burnt, not just get it turning. On whether it's worth fixing, you're in reasonable shape. If the engineer finds worn brushes, or brushes plus a cut-out, it's normally a modest repair and well worth doing even at 9 years. If the motor windings or the control board have gone, the cost gets close to a new budget machine, and replacing it is usually the better call at this age. 1. Find the full model number, usually on a sticker around the door opening or inside the door. It tells the engineer which motor and brushes it takes.
2. Optionally, if you're comfortable and it's unplugged, take off the back panel (a few screws) and look at the motor without touching any wiring. Scorch marks, black dust around the motor or melted connectors would back up the brushes or wiring theory. This is just for information to pass on; it doesn't change the need for the engineer to check it before use.
Understood, I'll keep it unplugged. The label inside the door reads IWC 71252. I took the back panel off and the plugs at the motor all look pushed in. I couldn't tell much else just by looking.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That's helpful. Connectors that look fully pushed home make a loose plug less likely, so the evidence still points most strongly at worn carbon brushes. I'd put that at fairly likely rather than certain. Close behind are a burnt-out motor winding or a tripped motor cut-out, which brushes can cause when they spark. A fault on the board's motor drive is the outside chance. 1. Look at the belt between the small motor pulley and the big drum pulley. If it's on and intact, that rules the belt out completely and helps the engineer.
2. On a brushed motor like those Indesits of this age typically use, there's a carbon brush holder on each side of the motor at the back end, each usually held by one screw with a small wire clipped on. Note which way round each goes, then ease one out and look at the carbon block. New brushes are roughly 3cm long. If yours are down to a stub of a centimetre or less, are chipped, or there's black dust and burn marks on the motor's copper segments, that suggests brushes as the cause. If they're still long and even, the motor winding, cut-out or board become more likely.
3. Refit them exactly as they came out, and don't power it up to test. Whatever you find, it still needs a qualified engineer to check it before it's used again, because of that burning smell. Worn brushes would mean the motor was arcing, and that sparking may have damaged the motor's copper segments or the wiring too. On your original question: if it's brushes, or brushes plus the cut-out, that's a modest repair and well worth doing on a 9-year-old machine with free, quiet bearings. If the engineer finds the motor windings or the control board have gone, a new budget machine is usually the better buy at this age. Let me know what the brushes and belt look like if you do have a peek.

I've had a look now. The belt is on both pulleys and feels tight. I took the two carbon brushes out: one is very short and blackened or charred at the tip, and the other is a bit longer. I don't own a multimeter, so I can't do any electrical tests.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That's a clear result, and it fits everything else. The belt being on and tight, plus no motor noise at all, rules the belt out. A brush worn very short and charred at the tip is a common sign of worn carbon brushes. Then the motor stops turning altogether. The uneven wear between the two brushes is common too. I'm fairly sure the carbon brushes are the likely faulty part. They're always replaced as a pair, never just the worn one. What isn't certain yet is whether the arcing has caused knock-on damage. 1. The motor's copper segments (the commutator) the brushes run on. Burn marks, pitting or deep grooves can mean new brushes won't last, and the motor may need attention.
2. The motor's thermal cut-out and windings, tested with a meter. Sparking and overheating can trip or damage the cut-out. That needs electrical testing, which isn't something you can do without a multimeter anyway. If you still have the back off and are curious, a look at those copper segments with a torch (still unplugged, no touching wiring) would give the engineer a useful heads-up. Either way, refit the brushes exactly as they came out, and leave it unplugged. Because of that burning smell, it does need a qualified engineer to check it before it's used again, even if new brushes are fitted. That's to confirm nothing else is scorched, not just to get it turning. It will save them time. On whether it's worth fixing: if it turns out to be just the brushes, or brushes plus the cut-out, that's a modest repair. If the engineer finds the commutator badly burnt or the windings gone, a new motor plus labour usually gets close to the cost of a new budget machine. At this age, replacing it would then be the more sensible choice.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
